result:
I want to write about the strange, quiet life of unfinished things.

Not abandoned things — that’s different — but the things left open on purpose, or by accident, or because life simply moved us forward before we could close the loop. A notebook with half a poem in it. A song stopped at the best chord. A conversation that ended too soon. A game saved and never reopened. A sketch with one eye drawn and the other left as a pale pencil ghost.

There’s something tender about them. They don’t demand completion the way they used to. They just wait, like rooms with the lights still on.

I think about how often we carry these unfinished things around without meaning to. A hobby we were sure would become part of our identity, until it wasn’t. A friendship that faded not with drama, but with silence. A version of ourselves we built in our heads at sixteen, at twenty, at twenty-five, who still lives somewhere in the background, wondering when we’ll come back to finish the job.

And yet maybe nothing is ever truly unfinished. Maybe some things are only meant to be begun.

A half-written story can still matter, not because it failed to become a whole book, but because for a little while it made you pay attention to language. A friendship that ended can still matter because, for a season, it shaped you. A dream you no longer pursue can still matter because it taught you what you wanted before you knew how to want it.

We tend to measure worth by completion. Did you finish it? Did you follow through? Did it become the thing it promised to become? But there’s another way to look at it: what did the unfinished thing give you while it was alive?

Sometimes starting is enough.
Sometimes beginning is the whole point.
Sometimes the most honest thing a person can do is make a small, imperfect mark and say, “I was here. I tried. I noticed. I cared enough to begin.”

I like that. I like that we are not only the sum of our finished projects. I like that we are also made of attempts. Of fragments. Of half-formed melodies and abandoned drafts and roads we turned away from. They are not failures. They are evidence of motion.

Maybe that’s why unfinished things feel so human. They remind us that we are always in the middle of becoming something else.

And perhaps that’s not a flaw.
Perhaps that’s the freedom.
